lessons.title: Introduction to Threads and Concurrency
lessons.description: Understand processes, threads, concurrency and parallelism in Java.
lessons.content:
Multithreading allows multiple threads of execution within a Java process. Threads share the process heap but have their own execution stacks.

A process is a running program with its own resources. A thread is an execution path within that process.

Concurrency means multiple tasks can make progress during overlapping periods. Parallelism means tasks execute simultaneously on different processing resources.

Multithreading is useful for responsive applications, background operations, network servers and processing independent tasks.

Java provides Thread, Runnable, Callable, ExecutorService and concurrency utilities.

Thread scheduling depends on the JVM and operating system. Execution order is not guaranteed.

Creating too many threads can increase memory use and context-switching overhead. Use appropriate thread pools and structured task management.

examples.title: Creating a Thread

lessons.title: Thread Creation, Runnable and Lifecycle
lessons.description: Create threads correctly and understand their lifecycle.
lessons.content:
Java threads can be created by extending Thread or by passing a Runnable to a Thread object.

Runnable represents a task with a run() method. Calling start() creates a new execution thread, while calling run() directly executes the method on the current thread.

Java Thread.State values include NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING and TERMINATED.

A RUNNABLE thread may be executing or waiting for CPU scheduling.

The join() method allows one thread to wait for another thread to finish.

sleep() pauses the current thread for at least approximately the requested duration, subject to scheduling and interruption.

A thread cannot be restarted after it has terminated. Calling start() more than once on the same Thread object throws IllegalThreadStateException.

Prefer separating task logic from thread management.

examples.explanation: Runs a task on a separate thread and waits for completion.

lessons.title: Synchronization and Race Conditions
lessons.description: Protect shared mutable data from concurrent access problems.
lessons.content:
A race condition occurs when a program's behavior depends on the timing of concurrent operations.

For example, count++ involves reading, modifying and writing a value. It is not an atomic operation.

The synchronized keyword provides mutual exclusion using an object's monitor. It also establishes memory visibility guarantees between properly synchronized operations.

A synchronized instance method locks the current object. A synchronized static method locks the corresponding Class object.

AtomicInteger provides atomic operations such as incrementAndGet() without requiring an explicit synchronized block for simple counters.

The volatile keyword provides visibility and ordering guarantees for a field, but it does not make compound operations such as count++ atomic.

Reduce shared mutable state where possible. Immutable objects and thread-safe collections can simplify concurrent programming.

examples.title: Thread-Safe Counter
examples.explanation: Uses AtomicInteger to increment a shared counter safely.

lessons.title: Deadlocks, Interruption and Thread Safety
lessons.description: Recognize common concurrency failures and manage thread cancellation.
lessons.content:
A deadlock occurs when threads wait indefinitely for resources held by one another.

A classic example involves Thread A holding Lock 1 while waiting for Lock 2, and Thread B holding Lock 2 while waiting for Lock 1.

Consistent lock ordering helps prevent deadlocks. Other approaches include reducing lock scope and using timed lock acquisition.

Thread interruption is a cooperative cancellation mechanism. Calling interrupt() sets the interruption status or causes certain blocking methods to throw InterruptedException.

When InterruptedException is caught and the method cannot propagate it, restoring the interruption status with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() is often appropriate.

Thread safety means shared objects behave correctly under concurrent access.

Common concurrency problems include race conditions, deadlocks, starvation and visibility errors.

Avoid holding locks during long-running or unpredictable operations when possible.

examples.title: Cooperative Interruption
examples.explanation: Stops a worker by interrupting its sleep and preserving interruption status.

lessons.title: ExecutorService, Callable and Concurrent Tasks
lessons.description: Manage multiple tasks using Java concurrency utilities.
lessons.content:
ExecutorService separates task submission from thread creation and scheduling.

A fixed thread pool reuses a bounded number of worker threads to execute submitted tasks.

Runnable represents a task that does not return a result. Callable<V> represents a task that returns a value and may throw a checked exception.

Submitting a Callable returns a Future<V>. Future.get() waits for completion and retrieves the result or reports task failure.

Always shut down an ExecutorService when it is no longer needed. shutdown() rejects new tasks while allowing previously submitted tasks to complete.

Java also provides concurrent collections such as ConcurrentHashMap and blocking queues such as LinkedBlockingQueue.

CompletableFuture supports composing asynchronous operations.

Real-world example: A placement platform can process independent report-generation jobs through an executor instead of manually managing one Thread per job.

quizzes.question: Which method starts a new Java thread of execution?
quizzes.explanation: Thread.start() schedules a new thread to execute its run() method. Calling run() directly does not create a new thread.

quizzes.question: Which interface defines a task with a run() method?
quizzes.explanation: Runnable defines the run() method and represents a task that does not return a result.

quizzes.question: Which method waits for another Thread object to finish execution?
quizzes.explanation: Thread.join() allows the calling thread to wait until the target thread terminates.

quizzes.question: What happens when start() is called twice on the same Thread object?
quizzes.explanation: A Java Thread instance can be started only once. Calling start() again throws IllegalThreadStateException.

quizzes.question: Why can count++ produce incorrect results when multiple threads update a shared counter?
options: The JVM disables arithmetic in threads
quizzes.explanation: count++ performs multiple steps that can interleave between threads, causing lost updates.

quizzes.question: Which Java utility provides atomic increment operations?
quizzes.explanation: AtomicInteger provides atomic methods such as incrementAndGet() for thread-safe counter updates.

quizzes.question: What is a deadlock?
options: Threads waiting indefinitely for resources held by one another
quizzes.explanation: Deadlock can occur when threads form a circular wait for locks or other resources.

quizzes.question: Which statement about volatile is correct?
options: It guarantees every method is synchronized
It provides visibility guarantees but not atomicity for compound updates
quizzes.explanation: volatile helps ensure visibility and ordering for field accesses, but compound updates such as count++ still require atomic operations or synchronization.

quizzes.question: Which interface represents a task that can return a result and throw a checked exception?
quizzes.explanation: Callable<V> defines call(), which can return a result and declare checked exceptions.

quizzes.question: What does ExecutorService.shutdown() do?
options: Stops accepting new tasks while allowing previously submitted tasks to complete
quizzes.explanation: shutdown() initiates an orderly shutdown. Previously submitted tasks are allowed to finish, and new tasks are rejected.

exercises.title: Run Three Download Tasks Concurrently
exercises.description: Create three independent threads using Runnable.
exercises.instructions: Write a Java program with three Runnable download simulations. Each task should print its filename, sleep for one second and print a completion message. Start all three threads before joining them. Observe that completion order is not guaranteed.

exercises.title: Explore Thread Lifecycle and join()
exercises.description: Observe thread states and wait for completion.
exercises.instructions: Create a worker Thread that performs a short task. Print its state before start(), immediately after start() and after join(). Explain why the intermediate state may vary between runs.

exercises.title: Fix a Shared Counter Race Condition
exercises.description: Protect shared mutable state from lost updates.
exercises.instructions: Create a shared counter incremented 10,000 times by each of two threads. First implement it using a plain int and observe possible incorrect results. Then fix it using AtomicInteger or synchronized. Wait for both threads to finish and verify the expected result of 20,000.

exercises.title: Build a Thread Pool Task Processor
exercises.description: Use ExecutorService and Future to manage tasks.
exercises.instructions: Create an ExecutorService with a fixed pool of three threads. Submit five Callable<Integer> tasks that return the square of their input. Collect the Future results, print them and shut down the executor in a finally block.

exercises.title: Debug a Two-Lock Deadlock
exercises.description: Identify circular lock acquisition and correct lock ordering.
exercises.instructions: Consider two locks, A and B. Thread 1 acquires A then B, while Thread 2 acquires B then A. Explain how deadlock can occur. Rewrite the locking logic so both threads acquire A before B. Explain why consistent ordering prevents this particular circular-wait deadlock.
